L'objectif : garder la qualité du Transformer tout en réduisant le coût sur les longs contextes. → Les fenêtres de contexte ont explosé. posts.content: Maxime Labonne View Maxime Labonne’s profile • 2nd Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI 3w • 3w Visible to everyone 🧲 Doc-to-LoRA: Turning documents to adapters! Long contexts are expensive. Every RAG system, every cached system prompt, every user preference file sitting in a context window is burning memory and adding latency. Context distillation is the principled fix, but it requires gradient updates per document, making it impractical for anything interactive or personalized. This paper takes a clean shot at the problem: → Instead of fine-tuning the LLM per document, they train a hypernetwork (Doc-to-LoRA) that reads a document once and outputs a LoRA adapter in a single forward pass, no backprop needed. → The hypernetwork uses a Perceiver-style cross-attention module, mapping variable-length token activations to a fixed-rank LoRA. Long docs are chunked and adapters are concatenated along the rank dimension, enabling generalization beyond the training context length. → On NIAH, D2L trained on 256-token sequences generalizes near-perfectly to 40K tokens at test time. Inference memory stays under 50MB regardless of haystack size, versus 12+ GB for the KV-cache baseline. → On SQuAD, D2L reaches ~82% of ICL performance with sub-second internalization latency and under 2GB VRAM, while vanilla CD needs 100+ seconds and 40+ GB. → A surprising zero-shot result: D2L transfers visual information from a VLM into a text-only LLM through adapter generation, with no explicit multimodal training. The approach is genuinely compelling, but the evaluation could be improved. Experiments use the (extremely) outdated Gemma-2-2B as the base model almost exclusively. We have no idea if the hypernetwork generalizes across different base architectures, or if training a new Doc-to-LoRA per model family kills the practical appeal. What I really want to see: can Doc-to-LoRA handle system prompt internalization robustly enough to replace static context in production deployments? Happy to hear your thoughts!

posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 2w • 2w Visible to everyone La plupart des équipes paient 4x trop cher pour leurs embeddings sans vraiment le savoir. Quand on a besoin d'embeddings le réflexe c'est de prendre text-embedding-ada-002 ou text-embedding-3-large à 1536 dimensions (voir plus). La logique derrière semble imparable : plus de dimensions = meilleure qualité. Mais la réalité est plus nuancée que cela. → Calculer la similarité cosine entre vecteurs à 384 dims est plus rapide qu'à 1536. → Stocker 10M vecteurs à 384 dims coûte moins cher (beaucoup) qu'à 1536. Et sur la majorité des use cases classiques (support client, knowledge base interne, documentation technique standard) : la différence de qualité de retrieval mesurée est très marginale. Pourquoi ça marche quand même avec des embeddings plus petits ? Grâce à Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). L'idée : entraîner le modèle de façon à ce que les premières dimensions condensent l'essentiel de la sémantique, les dimensions suivantes ne faisant qu'affiner, d'où l'image des poupées russes. Ainsi, un vecteur de 256 dims tiré d'un modèle MRL est aussi précis qu'un vecteur de 1536 dims d'une ancienne génération de modèles. OpenAI l'a intégré dans text-embedding-3, Nomic dans nomic-embed-text etc... En revanche il existe toujours des cas où les grandes dimensions restent intéressantes : → Documentation avec des variations de nomenclature très subtiles → Corpus multilingues denses → Bases hétérogènes où des faux positifs de similarité apparaissent à basse dimension Pour la grande majorité des cas vous pouvez commencer à 384. Mesurez, observez et tentez avec de plus grandes dimensions si les résultats ne vous semblent pas satisfaisants mais ne faites pas l'erreur de prendre les plus grandes dims sans tester les plus petites. _______ 📬 Veille Data/IA toutes les semaines – 15 min chrono : lebriefia.substack(.)com Je publie 3x par semaine sur l'IA, le machine learning et la data en général.

posts.content: Lan Chu View Lan Chu’s profile • 2nd AI Tech Lead | Senior Data Scientist | Work with LLMs before they were cool 3w • 3w Visible to everyone Remember our good friend BM25 that empowers every RAG hybrid search? We all know it is powerful but do you know how BM25 works exactly? It is a term-based retrieval method that improves upon TF-IDF, addressing issues with 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐡. 1. 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐤1 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫) If a document contains 100 occurrences of the term “computer,” is it twice as relevant as a document that contains 50 occurrences? Probably not. BM25 uses k1 to control diminishing returns. As term frequency increases, the score saturates, meaning additional occurrences contribute less and less to relevance. This prevents keyword stuffing from artificially inflating scores. 2. 𝐃𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐋𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐡 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐛 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫) If a document is very short and it contains “computer” once, that might already be a good indicator of relevance. But if the document is long and the term “computer” only appears once, it is likely that the document is not about computers. Long documents are more likely to contain many relevant terms, without making the document itself more relevant, leading to false positives. We want to give a reward to term matches to short documents and penalize the long ones. But what defines if a document is a short or a long one? BM25 uses the average corpus length (dl_avg) as a reference point. Documents longer than this average are considered long, while those shorter are considered short documents. → Short documents get rewarded for term matches → Long documents get penalized → The b parameter controls how strong this effect is. The higher the value of b, the higher the penalty for large documents. These two simple mechanisms make BM25 incredibly fasat and effective at finding relevant documents, which is why it is still the backbone of many modern retrieval systems. Are there other term-based retrieval methods that you are using?

posts.title: Adham Sersour View Adham Sersour’s profile • 1st Senior AI/ML Engineer 3w • 3w Visible to everyone The next trillion-dol
posts.content: Adham Sersour View Adham Sersour’s profile • 1st Senior AI/ML Engineer 3w • 3w Visible to everyone The next trillion-dollar AI company probably won't build a chatbot. It will build a model that can see your kitchen, hear "clean up," and physically do it. That model already exists, it worked in real apartments last year, and the architecture behind it is surprisingly simple to understand. I'll be honest, when I first stumbled on the term "VLA" a few months ago, I thought it was yet another acronym the AI hype machine invented to sound smart. Vision-Language-Action models. Sounds like something someone puts on a slide deck to justify a $600 million funding round. Then I actually dug into the research and something clicked, because VLAs represent the clearest progression I've seen in AI right now, and almost nobody outside the robotics community is paying attention. Here's what rewired my thinking. Your LLM is a brain in a jar. It can reason, plan, and compose, but it has no eyes, no hands, and no body. It lives entirely in the world of text. Researchers fixed this in two steps: first they gave it eyes (vision encoders that project images into the same token space the LLM already understands), and then they gave it hands (action outputs that generate motor commands from what it sees and hears). That's the LLM → VLM → VLA progression in one paragraph. A brain, then a brain that sees, then a brain that sees and acts in the physical world. Now here's where it gets interesting: the field can't agree on how to represent physical actions. One camp (Google's RT-2, OpenVLA) discretizes robot movements into tokens, same vocabulary trick as language. The other camp (Physical Intelligence's π₀) argues actions should stay continuous and uses flow matching to generate smooth trajectories directly. Both work, and the most interesting research right now is happening at their intersection. What made me take this seriously wasn't the tech demos though, it was the investment signals. Physical Intelligence raised $600M in their Series B, VLA papers at ICLR went from 9 to 164 in one year (that's 18×), and π₀.5 was tested in completely unseen San Francisco homes last April, not labs, actual apartments it had never seen, and it worked. The pattern underneath VLAs (extend a foundation model to new modalities and new output types) is the same pattern powering AI agents today. If you're building systems that take actions in digital environments, you're solving a version of the same architectural problem. I wrote a deeper breaking down the architecture, the two camps, and why the numbers say this is real and not hype. Link in comments. 5 resources if you want to go hands-on: → OpenVLA (open-source 7B, beat Google's 55B RT-2-X) → π₀ (open-sourced by Physical Intelligence) → NVIDIA GR00T N1 (humanoid VLA foundation model) → Open X-Embodiment (1M+ real robot trajectories, 34 labs) → HuggingFace LeRobot (the framework to start with) → UnifoLM-VLA — Unitree, open-source, built for the G1 → VLA 2.0 — XPeng, shared across robots, cars and drones on the same model

No chunking. No similarity search. Meet PageIndex, a vectorless, reasoning-based RAG system that retrieves like a human expert. It just hit 98.7% accuracy on FinanceBench, outperforming traditional vector RAG by a significant margin. Vector search finds what's semantically similar, but similarity is not relevance. When you're working with financial reports, legal filings, or technical manuals, you need reasoning, multi-step logic, and context across sections. A similarity score can't give you that. PageIndex thinks differently. It reads your document and builds a hierarchical tree index, like a table of contents but optimized for how LLMs actually think. Then it reasons through that tree to find what's actually relevant, the same way a human expert flips through a 200-page annual report. What that looks like in practice: • Documents stay in their natural structure, no artificial chunking • The LLM navigates the tree using reasoning, not pattern matching • Every answer comes with page and section references • No opaque embeddings, no "vibe retrieval" Works on SEC filings, legal documents, technical manuals, and academic papers. Anything that needs precision and exceeds your context window. Vector database RAG was the best we had. This is what we actually needed. Link to the GitHub repo in the comments.

Memento is a memory based continual learning framework for LLM agents that lets them learn from experience over time without touching model weights. It maintains a Case Bank of past trajectories including tasks, step sequences, tool usage, and outcomes. When a new task comes in, the agent plans and acts by pulling from similar past cases instead of starting from zero. Memento follows a planner and executor setup: 1. The Planner (an LLM) breaks the task into subtasks, retrieves relevant cases, and chooses a plan. 2. The Executor runs those subtasks using tools like search, code execution, or document processing through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), then logs the results back into memory. Key Features: • Memory based continual learning that improves agents through stored experience • Planner and executor architecture with case based reasoning for task decomposition • Unified tool ecosystem for search, code execution, document processing, media analysis and more • Learning without weight updates by retrieving and reusing relevant past cases • Strong results on long horizon and out of distribution tasks in reported benchmarks It is 100% open source. I finetuned a 20B parameter model gpt-oss in 1h30 minutes on a free GPU. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐩 • Model: OpenAI GPT-OSS 20B • Hardware: Free Colab T4 with 16GB VRAM • Technique: 4-bit quantization + LoRA adapters (rank=8) • Finetuning time: 90 minutes for 1 full epoch Unsloth is an optimization layer that works with HuggingFace Transformers + TRL and pytorch directly. 𝘚𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘥𝘦, 𝘴𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭𝘴, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 2-5𝘹 𝘧𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 70% 𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘮𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘺. 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐔𝐧𝐬𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫? Unsloth wrote their own GPU kernels together with a smarter gradient checkpointing implementation that uses ~30% less VRAM than the default. These optimizations apply whether you're doing LoRA or full fine-tuning. I tried running the same setup with pure HuggingFace to compare performance but hit multiple issues. First, gpt-oss is quantized in an MXFP4 format, which doesn't support backpropagation (it is an inference-only format). To train, you need to convert to something like BitsAndBytes NF4. Unsloth handles this conversion automatically. With vanilla HuggingFace, however, the only option is to dequantize back to bf16, which requires 65GB+ VRAM. The free T4 tier doesn’t have that much memory. But even if we try to load Unsloth’s BnB 4-bit version of the model directly with Huggingface, I still ran out of memory. Meaning that even with the same model weights, Unsloth's loading and memory management is much more efficient than pure HuggingFace. If you're experimenting with fine-tuning, Unsloth makes it easier than ever. posts.content: Benjamin Tardy View Benjamin Tardy’s profile • 2nd AI & ML Engineer 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Mon agent va envoyer un mail, mon agent va créer un ticket Jira, il va corriger ma MR. Mais avec quelles permissions ? Quand un agent fait appel à un MCP ou une API, au nom de qui le fait-il ? Avec quel token ? Comment on identifie qui a demandé quoi et à quel agent ? L'un des patterns qui émerge est le On-Behalf-Of (OBO). Au lieu de donner à l'agent vos identifiants et/ou un accès admin, on met en place une chaîne de délégation explicite. Vous autorisez l'agent à agir en votre nom avec des permissions précises, limitées dans le temps, et traçables. Les flows OAuth 2.0 actuels n'ont pas été conçus pour ça. Ils gèrent deux acteurs : un utilisateur et une application. Avec les agents, on passe à trois : l'utilisateur, l'application, et l'agent qui agit. Et c'est pour ça que l'IETF (l'organisme qui standardise les protocoles d'Internet) travaille en ce moment sur une extension OAuth dédiée aux agents IA. Un Internet Draft qui introduit deux nouveaux paramètres : requested_actor pour identifier quel agent demande l'accès, et actor_token pour qu'il prouve son identité lors de l'échange de tokens. Permission discovery, delegation chains, least-privilege, audit trails sont des sujets sur lesquels on peut parier, si vous avez peur que votre métier disparaisse. _______ 📬 Veille Data/IA toutes les semaines – 15 min chrono : lebriefia.substack(.)com Je publie 3x par semaine sur l'IA, le machine learning et la data en général.

Shipping daily in public. 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone 14 agentic coding lessons from the founder of OpenClaw, 🦄 Peter Steinberger. Who sold to OpenAI. I dug through every post on his blog. Ranked by how hard they hit. Save this. ⸻ 𝟭/ 𝗡𝗘𝗔𝗥 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗟𝗜𝗠𝗜𝗧𝗦, 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟𝗦 𝗣𝗔𝗡𝗜𝗖. Raw thinking leaks past 180K tokens. Compact early. Compact often. 𝟮/ "𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗬 𝗦𝗠𝗔𝗟𝗟 𝗕𝗢𝗠𝗕𝗦, 𝗡𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗙𝗔𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗡." Atomic commits. Something breaks? Roll back one commit. Not 40 files. 𝟯/ 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗞 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧'𝗦 𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘. It starts at zero. 100K+ lines, no context. I cut my CLAUDE md from 727 to 128 lines. Accuracy jumped. Let instruction files grow organically from real problems. Never architect upfront. 𝟰/ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗣 Stage 1: short prompts. "Fix this." Stage 2: eight-agent orchestration, 18 slash commands, custom workflows. You feel like a genius. Stage 3: back to short prompts. Elite looks like beginner. Most people are stuck in stage 2. Which stage are you in? Be honest. 𝟱/ 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗢𝗢 𝗟𝗢𝗡𝗚? 𝗬𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗔𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗧𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗚. I tested this. 4 out of 5 times the agent was forcing a feature my structure made hard. The fix wasn't a better prompt. It was a refactor. 𝟲/ 𝗖𝗟𝗜 𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗠𝗖𝗣𝘀. Every MCP injects its full schema into every prompt. Silent token tax. I found 81 tool definitions loading on every message. 𝟳/ 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗧𝗦, 𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗘𝗘𝗡𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗧𝗦. 50% of prompts should be screenshots. The rest? 1-2 sentences. Writing paragraphs? Still stage 2. 𝟴/ 𝗗𝗢𝗡'𝗧 𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖, 𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗖𝗨𝗦𝗦. Feed the model websites, screenshots, references. Ask "give me 3 options" before building anything. 𝟵/ 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞 𝗕𝗘𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗘𝗖𝗛. Stable APIs, more training data. Switching from niche libraries to standard ones cut my agent errors in half. 𝟭𝟬/ 𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗦 𝗔𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗔𝗣. 𝗗𝗢 𝗜𝗧 𝗢𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗡. Sonnet handles in 3 minutes what took me half a day. 20% of time should go to refactoring. jscpd, knip, ESLint. Agents clean their own mess on a schedule. 𝟭𝟭/ 𝟯𝟬𝟬𝗞 𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗘𝗦. 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗗𝗘𝗩. 𝟭𝟬𝟬% 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧-𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡. Steinberger: "I ship code I never read" 𝟭𝟮/ 𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗙𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗛. Build, test, move on. Wait a day and the agent starts from zero. 𝟭𝟯/ 𝗣𝗥 𝗥𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗘𝗪: 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧. First question: "Do you understand the intent of this PR?" Then point it to code it hasn't seen. Watch it connect dots. 𝟭𝟰/ "𝗩𝗜𝗕𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚" 𝗜𝗦 𝗔 𝗦𝗟𝗨𝗥. Tried it once, blamed the tool. posts.content: Patrick SZYMKOWIAK View Patrick SZYMKOWIAK’s profile • 3rd+ Founder / builder / RTK / Kexa 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone Début 2026, je brûlais mon forfait Claude Code en quelques heures. Pas à cause de prompts complexes. Juste du développement normal. Chaque commande que mon agent IA exécutait — git log, cargo test, ls -la — injectait des milliers de tokens inutiles dans la fenêtre de contexte. Des barres de progression. Des tests qui passent. Du formatage verbeux. Du bruit pur. Alors j'ai construit RTK — Rust Token Killer. En le développant, j'ai réalisé l'ampleur du problème : environ 80% des tokens consommés étaient du bruit. Un proxy CLI en Rust qui compresse les sorties de commandes AVANT qu'elles n'atteignent le contexte de l'agent IA. Mes vrais chiffres après 15 jours : → 7 061 commandes → 29.3M tokens en entrée → 4.8M en sortie → 24.6M tokens économisés (83.7%) Concrètement : - cargo test : 155 lignes → 3 lignes (98%) - git status : 119 caractères → 28 caractères - Sessions sensiblement plus longues - Les rate limits ? Beaucoup moins fréquents. Un seul binaire Rust. Zéro dépendance. Installation en une commande. Aujourd'hui, en 3 semaines, RTK c'est 521 ⭐ sur GitHub, 46 forks, ~1 000 utilisateurs actifs, et une compatibilité avec Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Aider, Codex, Windsurf et Cline. Si vous développez avec un agent IA et que vous sentez que ça rame ou que ça coupe, il y a de fortes chances que votre contexte soit saturé de bruit. Vous utilisez déjà RTK ? posts.title: A Practical Guide to Modern Document Understanding
posts.content: Markus Kuehnle View Markus Kuehnle’s profile • 2nd ML/AI Engineer | Building End-to-End Systems | Helping engineers ship AI from scratch to production 8mo • 8mo Visible to everyone Tesseract can’t answer: “What are the top 3 risks in this contract?” That’s where vision-language models take over. OCR still works.. but when context matters, it’s not enough. Let’s walk through the shift: 📌 𝟭. 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗰 𝗢𝗖𝗥 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱. You extract text → try to rebuild structure → hope it holds. But real documents aren’t clean: • Tables inside tables • Fonts and spacing that carry meaning • Layouts that don’t follow any order OCR is great for overlays, forms, and precise spans. It struggles when you need deeper understanding. 📌 𝟮. 𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆. PaLI is trained across 100+ languages. You give it a document image → it answers your question. “What’s the invoice total?” → “$1,294.55” It combines: • ViT (Vision Transformer) to encode the image • mT5 (Multilingual Text-to-Text Transformer) to generate the answer No text layer. No bounding boxes. Just reasoning over pixels. 📌 𝟯. 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝗴𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿: 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹 + 𝗩𝗤𝗔 ColPaLI = PaLI-Gemma + ColBERT-style retriever It: → Splits PDFs into visual pages → Encodes each page with token-wise embeddings → Retrieves relevant ones with late interaction → Answers based on the best-matching context Good for search + QA over large sets of scanned PDFs. 🧠 Bookmark this section if you're designing a doc understanding pipeline. 📌 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁? 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗢𝗖𝗥 𝗶𝗳: → You need precise fields, coordinates, or overlays → You’re doing form parsing or tabular extraction → You want full control, fast execution 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝗶𝗳: → You want end-to-end answers from document images → You deal with multilingual or unstructured scans → Layout context matters more than exact positions 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝗶𝗳: → You’re working with many PDFs, not just one → You need retrieval + VQA → You’re building document copilots or visual RAG systems The goal isn’t to replace OCR. It’s to know when OCR is not enough. PaLI and ColPaLI bring in context, layout, and reasoning and open up new ways to work with documents that don’t follow rules. 💬 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗣𝗮𝗟𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝗹𝗸𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 ↓ Curious what you’d build with it. ♻️ Repost to help someone in your network. posts.content: Paolo Perrone View Paolo Perrone’s profile • 2nd No BS AI/ML Content | ML Engineer with a Plot Twist 🥷100M+ Views 📝 1mo • 1mo Visible to everyone They told you 70B models need 80GB VRAM. They lied. AirLLM runs Llama 70B on a 4GB GPU. No quantization. No distillation. No pruning. The trick: layer-wise inference. Instead of loading the entire model into VRAM, it loads one layer at a time from disk. Your GPU only ever holds one layer. The rest lives on disk. What you can run: → Llama 70B on 4GB VRAM → Llama 405B on 8GB VRAM → Qwen2.5, Mixtral, ChatGLM all supported pip install airllm from airllm import AutoModel model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("garage-bAInd/Platypus2-70B-instruct") input_tokens = model.tokenizer(input_text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=128) output = model.generate( input_tokens['input_ids'].cuda(), max_new_tokens=20) Standard transformers API. That's it. Optional: 4-bit compression for 3x speed boost. model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("...", compression='4bit') Trade-off: slower inference than full VRAM loading. But if you don't have the VRAM, you don't have options. Works on MacOS with Apple Silicon too. 1.9k GitHub stars. Apache 2.0. → github.com/lyogavin/airllm 💾 Save for when your GPU budget doesn't match your model ambitions ♻️ Repost if you've ever closed a tab because "requires 80GB VRAM"

What's the difference? Recently there have been many MCP vs. Function Calling articles floating around. Let’s simplify. ❗️ 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹: Function Calling and Tool Use in Agentic Systems are almost the same thing. You can implement tools via functions, the only difference is that functions are usually used to enforce stricter structure to the input and output schema. User Query is passed to the Agent (usually a Python application). 𝟮. The application implements MCP Client and via it retrieves all available tools from the MCP servers. 𝟯. posts.content: Michel Antônio Gonçalves View Michel Antônio Gonçalves’ profile • 3rd+ Data Developer at CI&T 3mo • 3mo Visible to everyone In BigQuery, LIMIT limits your results, but not your bill It felt bizarre: I would add LIMIT 1000, LIMIT 100, or even LIMIT 10 in BigQuery, yet the query would still scan over 100GB. For newcomers, especially those tasked with validating data directly in production, this is a terrifying rite of passage. Unlike traditional row-based databases like Postgres or MySQL, LIMIT in BigQuery does not reduce the volume of data scanned from disk. It scans the entire column first and only then discards the extra rows to give you your 10 lines. It's like paying for the full buffet, but only getting to eat a fraction of the salad. This is where TABLESAMPLE becomes a life-saver and, literally, a money-saver. Unlike LIMIT, using TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1 PERCENT) instructs the execution engine to scan only a random sample of data blocks. If your table is 1tb: With LIMIT 10 / 100 / 1000: You could still process the full 1tb. With TABLESAMPLE (1%): You only process around 10gb. The bottom line is: if you just need to check the "shape" of the data or test a logic, stop relying on LIMIT and start using TABLESAMPLE. The budget will thank you! #BigQuery #DataEngineering #GoogleCloud #DataAnalytics #SQLTips #CloudOptimization

posts.content: Shirin Khosravi Jam View Shirin Khosravi Jam’s profile • 2nd Sr. Data Scientist/ AI Engineer | Data Science, RAG, AI Agents, & MLOps | Germany’s Top Female Voice in AI (Favikon) 🇩🇪 | 235k+ AI/ML Community 🤯 | Opinions are my own! 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone 69.99% of AI Engineers don't know how to structure a repo This is how you can structure your GenAI repo 👇 Here’s how we structure production-grade FastAPI based GenAI systems: 🔹 𝘀𝗿𝗰/ - 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 We use a layered + domain-first architecture - the same structure that powers robust ML/AI systems in production. Let’s break it down: 1️⃣ 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀/ → SQLAlchemy ORM models ↳ Defines your database schema: tables, types, indexes ↳ E.g. academic paper metadata: title, authors, abstract 2️⃣ 𝘀𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘀/ → Pydantic models for data validation ↳ Type-safe request/response structures ↳ Handles optional fields, default values, constraints 3️⃣ 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀/ → FastAPI route definitions ↳ Logical grouping of endpoints (e.g., /search, /upload) ↳ Auto-generates clean Swagger/OpenAPI docs ✅ Exposes your system cleanly to devs, tools, and UIs. 4️⃣ 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀/ → DB interaction layer ↳ Clean abstraction over SQL queries ↳ Makes business logic readable + testable ✅ No raw SQL scattered in your app. Easy to test and evolve. 5️⃣ 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀/ - The brain of your application → Logic organized by domain, not just CRUD e.g.: ↳ opensearch/ → Hybrid retrieval logic ✅ Modular by design: swap, extend, or evolve features without chaos. 6️⃣ 𝗱𝗯/ → Database engine config ↳ Connection pooling, retry logic, async sessions ✅ Rock-solid DB handling. No “random connection errors” in prod. 7️⃣ 𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻.𝗽𝘆 → FastAPI entry point ↳ Imports routes, applies middlewares, sets up CORS + logging ✅ Single source of truth for app startup. 8️⃣ 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀.𝗽𝘆 / 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀.𝗽𝘆 → Reliability and observability layer ↳ Logs tracebacks ↳ Converts random errors into structured API messages ✅ Debugging and monitoring become predictable. 🔹 𝗕𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗿𝗰/: 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮 + 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 1️⃣ 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 + 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲.𝘆𝗺𝗹 → One-line infra bootstrapping: ↳ Starts: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, Airflow, Ollama ✅ Works on every machine. No setup nightmares. 2️⃣ 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 → Simplifies commands like: ↳ make test, make lint, make up, etc. ✅ Standardized developer workflows. 3️⃣ 𝗽𝗿𝗲-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴 . 𝘆𝗮𝗺𝗹 → Linting + formatting (Ruff, Black, isort) → Prevents bad code from being committed ✅ Clean code. Enforced automatically. 4️⃣ 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀/ → Pytest structure ↳ Unit tests with fixtures and mocks ✅ You can confidently refactor without breaking things. 5️⃣ 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀/ → Analysis or test notebooks PS: As you put the repo into production there would more components added, e.g. CI/CD, infrastructure, etc. Want to see it in action? posts.content: Brij kishore Pandey View Brij kishore Pandey’s profile • 2nd AI Architect & Engineer | AI Strategist 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone Most Generative AI projects don’t fail because of weak models — they fail because the engineering foundation is weak. Teams often begin with prompts, APIs, and notebooks. But when it’s time to scale, integrate, audit, or productionize, everything starts to break. What really decides if your AI project moves from demo to product? How well it is structured from day one. The visual you see is a structured Generative AI project layout. It covers modularity, maintainability, configuration management, prompt engineering, token usage, and logging. It helps solve common challenges like: • Unstructured notebooks and prototype chaos • Hardcoded prompts and model settings • No token tracking, caching, or rate limiting • Mixing prompt logic with core application code • Difficulty moving from proof-of-concept to production What this structure includes effectively: • YAML-based configurations for prompts, models, and logging • Modular LLM clients (GPT, Claude, Base) • Prompt engineering utilities: templates, chaining, few-shot design • Token counting, caching, logging, and rate limiters • Separate example scripts and experimental notebooks • Clear separation between utilities, handlers, and core logic What is not included — but should be added in any production-ready GenAI system: Security and Governance • Secret management (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) • PII handling and compliance safeguards • Guardrails, content moderation, responsible use Observability and Monitoring • Token usage analytics and latency tracking • Failure metrics, tool-call history, retry insights • Integration with LangSmith, Honeycomb, or Arize Testing and Evaluation • Prompt regression testing • Response quality evaluation frameworks (RAGAS, TruLens) • Model behaviour tracking across iterations Agent, Memory, and Context Management • Memory layers (short-term, long-term, vector-based) • Agent orchestration with structured task flows • Document retrieval, tool routing, function handlers Ops and Deployment • CI/CD and container orchestration • Scalable API deployment (FastAPI, Lambda, Kubernetes) • API gateway, authentication, throttling, access control This framework is a great start. But scaling GenAI is less about prompts—and more about disciplined engineering. Structure is not just documentation. In AI systems, structure itself is a feature. The complete GitHub template code for this structure is available in the comments.

posts.content: Abi Aryan ☯︎ View Abi Aryan ☯︎’s profile • 2nd ML Research Engineer | Author: LLMOps & GPU Engineering | Making AI Systems go brrrr... 4mo • 4mo Visible to everyone So many people keep asking me this ⁣“𝘢𝘣𝘪, 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘨𝘱𝘶 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘐 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘮𝘺 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 AI 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘫𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘴 𝘢𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘮𝘦” so i just dumped everything in one table.. No affiliate links, no one sponsored this (hi NVIDIA hi AMD hi Intel Corporation 😂 👋). I can assure you I still have a lot of a little bit of soul left in me 😝 ⁣𝖶𝖾𝗅𝗅, 𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗎𝖺𝗅𝗅𝗒 𝗂𝗍'𝗌 𝖺 𝖽𝗋𝖺𝖿𝗍 𝖿𝗋𝗈𝗆 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗑 𝗈𝖿 𝗆𝗒 𝖦𝖯𝖴 𝖤𝗇𝗀𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀 𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗄 𝗍𝗁𝖺𝗍 𝖨 𝖺𝗆 𝖼𝗎𝗋𝗋𝖾𝗇𝗍𝗅𝗒 𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗇𝗀..⁣ So key Takeaways on GPU Performance for LLMs: - 𝟒𝟎𝟗𝟎⁣⁣ is still my preferred starter. - 𝐑𝐓𝐗 𝐀𝟔𝟎𝟎𝟎 (𝟒𝟖 𝐆𝐁 𝐄𝐂𝐂, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟐): It can handle very large models like 130B (Q5) or 405B (Q3) on a single card, assuming optimized frameworks and reasonable batch sizes. Still viable for daily use. - 𝐑𝐓𝐗 𝟓𝟎𝟗𝟎: Extremely fast, achieving ~120–140 tokens/sec on 70B Q6, but 32 GB VRAM can be limiting for models that previously ran on 48 GB. High speed, lower memory capacity trade-off. Do not recommend. - 𝐑𝐗 𝟕𝟗𝟎𝟎 𝐗𝐓𝐗: Offers VRAM comparable to a 4090 at a lower cost. ROCm software support has improved significantly, making it a more practical AMD option for LLMs, though CUDA remains more optimized. - 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐥 𝐀𝐫𝐜 𝐁𝟓𝟖𝟎: Surprisingly capable for medium-sized models like 70B Q4. A cost-effective option for those on a budget, though driver maturity and ecosystem support are still developing. - 𝐇𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐨-𝟖𝐋: Ultra low-power option for smaller models (~7B). Achieves 35–40 tokens/sec at ~4 watts, ideal for always-on, energy-efficient deployment. I still suggest AMD mostly for racks and SLMs, 𝐈'𝐥𝐥 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐦𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐲𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭. Treat this as your rough guide, hope it helps someone. Enjoy!
